stories.summary: Africa: From Commonwealth Connections to Economic Opportunity - Expanding AfricaâCaribbean Trade Linkages 30 October 2026 allAfrica.com guest column By Hon Shirley Botchwey, Commonwealth Secretary-General; Dr George Elombi, President and Chairman of the Board of Directors, African Export-Import Bank; and Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director, International Trade Centre When Commonwealth leaders gather in Antigua and Barbuda this November, they will confront rising trade tensions, geopolitical shocks and supply chain disruption alongside longstanding challenges, such as high debt, limited affordable finance, climate exposure and poor connectivity. Across Africa, the Pacific and the Caribbean, these pressures make diversifying markets, attracting productive investment and building resilience through trade even more urgent. They also increase the importance of regional and cross-regional value chains that can withstand disruptions to established trade relationships. One opportunity lies in plain sight: stronger Africa-Caribbean economic connections. Shared history, culture and diaspora relationships provide a foundation, as do common ambitions to diversify exports, add value locally and create opportunities for small businesses, including those led by women and young entrepreneurs.

The reversal comes after CAF reviewed its earlier plan to move AFCON to a four-year schedule and introduce an Africa Nations League as a biennial competition. CAF said the proposed Nations League would take several years to generate the financial resources and football development benefits required to make its competitions globally competitive and financially sustainable. He said the Finance Ministry could meet the legal deadline but that doing so would leave it unable to produce a comprehensive revenue forecast or make the best use of the money. The request came in a communication to House Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, read during Thursday's plenary session. Boakai wrote that the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning had told him the statutory deadline under the Public Financial Management Law could be met. Submitting on time, the ministry said, could undermine the government's ability to forecast revenue fully and to make "optimal and efficient allocations" across the country's many priorities. "I therefore seek your understanding and concurrence as we finalize the processes to ensure the draft national budget for fiscal year 2027 is submitted to the Legislature on November 6, 2026," Boakai said.

ICN chief executive Howard Catton said the "tragic news" was a reminder that prevalent misinformation was particularly dangerous for healthcare staff after young men armed with machetes killed the nurse. "Health misinformation and the breakdown of trust in science is now a deadly risk for nurses and health workers," Catton posted on the media platform X on Oct. 29. The UN's Ebola coordinator and the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) on Oct. 29 deplored the killing of the nurse working to fight the disease in the DRC four days earlier. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn In an interview with AllAfrica, Catton also warned that community health workers often supplant nurses and may be seen as an easy, cheap substitute for a skilled nursing workforce in parts of Africa. "There is both the migration of registered nurses from the continent of Africa and unemployment of nurses in Africa," said Catton. "So, as we see this growth in community health workers, we also know that registered nurses continue to leave Africa for high-income countries in Europe or North America." At the same time, many nurses on the continent remain unemployed. Catton cited UN figures showing Africa's health workforce grew to 5.72 million in 2024, up from 4.3 million in 2018, noting that such progress is not keeping pace with demand.

A federal jury in Boston found that Nshimiye concealed his alleged participation in attacks against the Tutsi community while testifying in the 2019 immigration fraud trial of his former university classmate, Jean Leonard Teganya. Nshimiye fled Rwanda for Kenya in 1994 and was admitted to the U.S. as a refugee the following year. Evidence presented at his trial showed that, while a student at the University of Rwanda in Butare, he took part in attacks on the Tutsi people, including by striking them on the head with a club. Nshimiye faces up to five years in prison for each of four perjury counts and up to 10 years for obstruction of justice.

"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict. Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training. The M23 has seized mineral-rich areas, including gold-mining sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area in North Kivu.

stories.title: Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
stories.summary: Image caption, Neema Munuo, whose 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami was shot dead on the day of the election, wants the government to acknowledge her suffering By Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Dar es Salaam ,Â Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Lucy Fleming Published 29 October 2026 Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured. "We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC. On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear". The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded. Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing. He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials. As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths , Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies. “We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment. “It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

stories.title: Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5OfLK Prefer DW on Google Senegal is hoping to make Africa's historic moment count beyond the next two weeks Image: Fatma Esma Arslan Ozdel/Anadolu/IMAGO Advertisement On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports. Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future. "I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW. "I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here." Senegal gears up for Youth Olympic Games To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video An historic Games for Senegal and Africa The 2026 Youth Games in Senegal will also be a first beyond the history it is making in Africa. "Of the 2,700 athletes who will be competing in Dakar, there will be a 50-50 split between men and women," Olivia Nloga, Chief Brand Promotion Officer on the organizing committee, told DW. "But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists." Several sports are also making their debut at the Youth Olympic Games, such as five-a-side baseball, kung fu and the Senegalese specialty of beach wrestling.

stories.title: Africa: Wcaf V - African Development Bank Group and UK Export Finance Sign MOU to Mobilise Financing for Africa
stories.summary: Wcaf V - African Development Bank Group and UK Export Finance Sign MOU to Mobilise Financing for Africa 23 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The African Development Bank Group (AfDB) and UK Export Finance (UKEF), the United Kingdom's export credit agency, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen cooperation on co-financing projects across Africa and mobilise additional resources for the continent's sustainable development. Abdul Kamara, Officer in Charge, Vice President of the African Development Bank Group, and Tim Reid, Chief Executive of UK Export Finance, signed the agreement on 21 October in Conakry, Guinea, on the sidelines of the fifth UK-West and Central Francophone Africa Trade and Investment Forum (WCAF V). It is the first framework agreement between the two institutions. "Africa's financing needs call for partnerships that bring additional capital to the continent at scale. This agreement with UK Export Finance gives our cooperation a structured framework and opens new opportunities to finance the infrastructure and investments that will drive Africa's growth," said Abdul Kamara, OIC Vice President of the African Development Bank Group . The Memorandum of Understanding provides a framework for the two institutions to identify, assess and develop co-financing opportunities for sovereign and non-sovereign operations in the Bank's regional member countries, drawing on each institution's financial instruments.

stories.title: Paddy Donnelly obituary
stories.summary: Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa View image in fullscreen Paddy Donnelly came to London from South Africa in the early 80s to work for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa Obituary Paddy Donnelly obituary My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity. In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive. He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda , Kenya and now Nigeria.
